reference_title: Wood Handbook: Wood as an Engineering Material (USDA Forest Products Laboratory, General Technical Report FPL-GTR-282, 2021)

sections.title: Nails
sections.summary: Nails: withdrawal of common wire nails (Eq. 8-1a/b) and annularly threaded nails (Eq. 8-2a/b); pre-1991 lateral resistance p = K D^(3/2) (printed as Eq. 8-2, Table 8-4); post-1991 yield model (Table 8-5) with the nail dowel bearing strength Fe = 114.5 G^1.84 (Eq. 8-3a/b); spacing, moisture effects and load-slip models (Eq. 8-4 to 8-8).
sections.body: [p. 8-1] Maximum lateral resistance and safe design load values for small-diameter (nails, spikes, and wood screws) and large-diameter dowel-type fasteners (bolts, lag screws, and drift pins) were based on an empirical method prior to 1991; lateral resistance values are currently based on a yield model theory, adapted for the 1991 edition of the National Design Specification for Wood Construction (NDS). The chapter calls the empirical method pre-1991 and the theoretical method post-1991. Withdrawal resistance methods have not changed, so the pre- and post-1991 refer only to lateral resistance. The research results of this chapter are often modified for structural safety, based on judgment or experience, and thus information presented in design documents may differ from information presented in this chapter. Most load equations presented in the nail section apply for bright, smooth, common steel wire nails driven into wood when there is no visible splitting (nail types, Fig. 8-1). [p. 8-2] Penny sizes, although still widely used, are obsolete; specifying nail sizes by length and diameter dimensions is recommended (Tables 8-1 to 8-3). Withdrawal: for bright common wire nails driven into the side grain of seasoned wood or unseasoned wood that remains wet, the maximum withdrawal load is given by the empirical equation p = 54.12 G^(5/2) D L (metric) (Eq. 8-1a); p = 7,850 G^(5/2) D L (inch-pound) (Eq. 8-1b), where p is maximum load (N, lb), L depth (mm, in.) of penetration of the nail in the member holding the nail point, G specific gravity of the wood based on ovendry weight and volume at 12% moisture content (see Chap. 5, Tables 5-2 to 5-5), and D diameter of the nail (mm, in.). (The NDS uses ovendry weight and volume as a basis.) The loads expressed by Equation (8-1) represent average data. [p. 8-3] Effect of seasoning: if common smooth-shank nails are driven into green wood that is allowed to season, or into seasoned wood that is subjected to cycles of wetting and drying before the nails are pulled, they lose a major part of their initial withdrawal resistance. The withdrawal resistance for nails driven into wood that is subjected to changes in moisture content may be as low as 25% of the values for nails tested soon after driving. Where resistance is regained or even increased under some conditions of moisture variation and time, such sustained performance should not be relied on in the design of a nailed joint. [p. 8-4] For bright annularly threaded nails, with shank-to-thread-crest diameter difference greater than 0.2 mm (0.008 in.) and thread spacing between 1.27 mm (0.05 in.) and 1.96 mm (0.077 in.), driven in the side grain of seasoned wood, the immediate maximum withdrawal load is given by the empirical equation p = 77.57 G^2 D L (metric) (Eq. 8-2a); p = 11,250 G^2 D L (inch-pound) (Eq. 8-2b), where G is specific gravity based on ovendry weight and volume and oven dry moisture content and D the shank diameter of the nail. The expression is valid only for the threaded portion of the nail. Comparison of Equations (8-1) and (8-2) indicates that the bright annularly threaded nail can have withdrawal resistances that are double the values of common nails. [p. 8-6] Lateral resistance, pre-1991: test loads at joint slips of 0.38 mm (0.015 in.) (approximate proportional limit load) for bright common wire nails driven into the side grain of seasoned wood are expressed by the empirical equation p = K D^(3/2) (printed as Eq. 8-2, the same number as the threaded-nail withdrawal equation above), where p is lateral load per nail, K a coefficient (Table 8-4) and D diameter of the nail. The loads given by the equation apply only where the side member and the member holding the nail point are of approximately the same density. The thickness of the side member should be about one-half the depth of penetration of the nail in the member holding the point. To maintain a sufficient ratio between ultimate load and the load at 0.38 mm (0.015 in.), the nail should penetrate into the member holding the point by not less than 10 times the nail diameter for dense woods (specific gravity greater than 0.61) and 14 times the diameter for low-density woods (specific gravity less than 0.42), with straight-line interpolation between. Post-1991: the yield model theory selects the worst case of yield modes based on different possibilities of wood bearing and nail bending. It does not account for nail head effects, friction between the main and side member, or axial forces transmitted along the length of the fastener (Fig. 8-5). [p. 8-7] Table 8-5 gives the 5% offset lateral yield strength Z for nails and screws in a two-member joint: mode Is D ts Fes; mode IIIm k1 D p Fem/(1 + 2Re) (nails only); mode IIIs k2 D ts Fem/(2 + Re) for nails and k3 D ts Fem/(2 + Re) for screws; mode IV D^2 times the square root of 2 Fem Fyb/(3(1 + Re)) for nails and of 1.75 Fem Fyb/(3(1 + Re)) for screws, with Re = Fem/Fes. Mode I is a wood bearing failure in either the main or side member; mode II is a rotation of the fastener in the joint without bending; modes III and IV are a combination of wood bearing failure and one or more plastic hinge yield formations in the fastener. Modes Im and II have not been observed in nail and spike connections. The yield model theory is applicable to all types of dowel fasteners (nails, screws, bolts, lag screws), and thus the wood bearing capacity is described by a material property called the dowel bearing strength. The dowel bearing strength of the wood is experimentally determined by compressing a dowel into a wood member; the strength basis is the load representing a 5% diameter offset on the load-deformation curve (Fig. 8-4). Dowel bearing strength Fe (MPa, lb in^-2) is empirically related to specific gravity G by Fe = 114.5 G^1.84 (metric) (Eq. 8-3a); Fe = 16,600 G^1.84 (inch-pound) (Eq. 8-3b), where specific gravity is based on ovendry weight and volume (the exponent is printed as "1 84", the decimal point not shown). Screws use this same equation (p. 8-12); bolts have their own, Eq. 8-17 and 8-18 (p. 8-19), and lag screws use the bolt equations (p. 8-14). Bending yield strengths for the common nails are determined by ASTM F1575 tests with typical values ranging between 551 MPa (80,000 lb in^-2) and 689 MPa (100,000 lb in^-2) for common nails. Smaller diameter nails have higher bending yield strength due to surface hardening during fabrication. Spacing: end distance, edge distance, and spacing of nails should be such as to prevent unusual splitting. As a general rule, nails should be driven no closer to the edge of the side member than one-half its thickness and no closer to the end than the thickness of the piece. [p. 8-8] When nails are driven into the end grain, limited data on softwood species indicate that their maximum resistance to lateral displacement is about two-thirds that for nails driven into the side grain; individual end-grain results are more erratic, and the minimum loads approach only 75% of corresponding values for side-grain nailing. To prevent excessive deformation, lateral loads obtained for seasoned wood should be reduced by 25% for unseasoned wood that will remain wet or be loaded before seasoning takes place. Structural joints should be inspected at intervals, and if it is apparent that the joint has loosened during drying, the joint should be reinforced with additional nails. Load-slip: a theoretical model treating the nail as a beam on an elastic foundation gives the initial slope of the load-slip curve (Eq. 8-4, 8-5); for seasoned wood the elastic bearing constant is k0 = 582 G (metric) (Eq. 8-6a), 2,144,000 G (inch-pound) (Eq. 8-6b) if no lead hole is used, and k0 = 869 G (metric) (Eq. 8-7a), 3,200,000 G (inch-pound) (Eq. 8-7b) with a prebored lead hole equal to 90% of the nail diameter; empirical models of the whole curve include P = A log10(1 + B delta) (Eq. 8-8a) and a model with a load-reducing behavior (Eq. 8-8b).
key_points: Common wire nail withdrawal, side grain of seasoned wood or unseasoned wood that remains wet: p = 54.12 G^(5/2) D L (metric), Eq. 8-1a; 7,850 G^(5/2) D L (inch-pound), Eq. 8-1b (p. 8-2)
Withdrawal resistance for nails in wood subjected to moisture content changes may be as low as 25% of the values soon after driving; regained resistance should not be relied on in design (p. 8-3)
Annularly threaded nail withdrawal: p = 77.57 G^2 D L (metric), Eq. 8-2a, for thread crest difference > 0.2 mm and thread spacing 1.27 to 1.96 mm; valid only for the threaded portion (p. 8-4)
Pre-1991 lateral load at 0.38 mm slip: p = K D^(3/2), printed as Eq. 8-2, K from Table 8-4; applies only where side and main members are of approximately the same density (p. 8-6)
Nail dowel bearing strength: Fe = 114.5 G^1.84 (metric), Eq. 8-3a (p. 8-7); screws use the same equation (p. 8-12); bolts use Eq. 8-17 and 8-18 (p. 8-19); lag screws use the bolt equations (p. 8-14)
Table 8-5: yield mode equations (Is, IIIm, IIIs, IV) for nails and screws in a two-member joint; mode IV has 2 for nails and 1.75 for screws (p. 8-7)
Lateral loads for seasoned wood should be reduced by 25% for unseasoned wood that will remain wet or be loaded before seasoning (p. 8-8)
sections.applicability: Sizing and checking nailed connections for withdrawal and lateral (shear) loading.

sections.title: Spikes, Staples, and Drift Bolts
sections.summary: Spikes use the nail equations (withdrawal penetration less two-thirds of the point length); staples have been estimated with the nail equations without verification; drift bolt withdrawal p = 45.51 G^2 D L (Eq. 8-9a/b).
sections.body: [p. 8-9] Spikes: common wire spikes are manufactured in the same manner as common wire nails, with a chisel or diamond point, in lengths of 76 to 305 mm (3 to 12 in.). The withdrawal and lateral resistance equations and limitations given for common wire nails are also applicable to spikes, except that in calculating the withdrawal load for spikes, the depth of penetration is taken as the length of the spike in the member receiving the point, minus two-thirds the length of the point. Staples: most factors that affect the withdrawal and lateral loads of nails similarly affect the loads on staples. Equation (8-1) has been used to predict the withdrawal load for one leg of a staple, but no verification tests have been done. The load in lateral resistance varies approximately as the 3/2 power of the diameter; the diameter of each leg of a two-legged staple must therefore be about two-thirds the diameter of a nail to provide a comparable load. [p. 8-10] Equation (8-2) has been used to predict the lateral resistance of staples. However, yield model theory equations have not yet been experimentally verified for staples. Corrosion, sustained performance under service conditions, and durability in various uses should be considered in evaluating the relative usefulness of a stapled connection. Drift bolts: a drift bolt (or drift pin) is a long pin of iron or steel, with or without head or point, driven into a bored hole through one timber and into an adjacent one. The ultimate withdrawal load of a round drift bolt or pin from the side grain of seasoned wood is given by p = 45.51 G^2 D L (metric) (Eq. 8-9a); p = 6,600 G^2 D L (inch-pound) (Eq. 8-9b), where p is the ultimate withdrawal load (N, lb), G specific gravity based on the ovendry weight and volume at 12% moisture content of the wood, D diameter of the drift bolt (mm, in.), and L length of penetration of the bolt (mm, in.).
key_points: Spikes: the nail withdrawal and lateral equations and limitations apply, with withdrawal penetration taken as the length in the member receiving the point minus two-thirds the length of the point (p. 8-9)
Staples: Eq. 8-1 and 8-2 have been used for staples, but without verification tests; yield model equations have not been experimentally verified for staples (p. 8-9, 8-10)
Drift bolt or pin ultimate withdrawal: p = 45.51 G^2 D L (metric), Eq. 8-9a; 6,600 G^2 D L (inch-pound), Eq. 8-9b (p. 8-10)
sections.applicability: Heavy-timber connections (drift bolts/pins) and sheathing attachment (spikes, staples).

sections.title: Wood Screws
sections.summary: Wood screw withdrawal p = 108.25 G^2 D L (Eq. 8-10a/b) for the screw sizes of Table 8-8; particleboard torque and withdrawal (Eq. 8-11, 8-12); pre-1991 lateral resistance p = K D^2 (Eq. 8-13); post-1991 yield model with the nail dowel bearing equation (Eq. 8-3).
sections.body: [p. 8-10] Ultimate test values for withdrawal loads of wood screws inserted into the side grain of seasoned wood may be expressed as p = 108.25 G^2 D L (metric) (Eq. 8-10a); p = 15,700 G^2 D L (inch-pound) (Eq. 8-10b), where p is maximum withdrawal load (N, lb), G specific gravity based on ovendry weight and volume at 12% moisture content, D shank diameter of the screw (mm, in.), and L length of penetration of the threaded part of the screw (mm, in.). [p. 8-11] These values are based on reaching ultimate load in 5 to 10 min. This equation is applicable when screw lead holes have a diameter of about 70% of the root diameter of the threads in softwoods, and about 90% in hardwoods. The equation values are applicable to the screw sizes listed in Table 8-8. For lengths and gauges outside these limits, the actual values are likely to be less than the equation values. The withdrawal loads of screws inserted in the end grain of wood are somewhat erratic, but when splitting is avoided, they should average 75% of the load sustained by screws inserted in the side grain. Particleboard: the maximum torque before the threads are stripped is T = 3.16 + 0.0096X (metric) (Eq. 8-11a), T = 27.98 + 1.36X (inch-pound) (Eq. 8-11b), for 8-gauge screws with 15.9 mm (5/8 in.) penetration; ultimate withdrawal is P = K D^(1/2) (L - D/3)^(5/4) G^2 (Eq. 8-12), with K = 41.1 (face) and 31.8 (edge) metric, 2,655 and 2,055 inch-pound, and for fiberboard K = 57.3 and 44.3 metric (3,700 and 2,860 inch-pound). Lateral resistance, pre-1991: proportional limit loads for wood screws in the side grain of seasoned wood are given by the empirical equation p = K D^2 (Eq. 8-13), K from Table 8-4, shank diameters by gauge in Table 8-9. Equation (8-13) applies when the depth of penetration of the screw into the block receiving the point is not less than seven times the shank diameter and when the side member and the main member are approximately of the same density. The thickness of the side member should be about one-half the depth of penetration of the screw in the member holding the point. The end distance should be no less than the side member thickness, and the edge distances no less than one-half the side member thickness. [p. 8-12] When the screw holds metal to wood, the load can be increased by about 25%. Screws should always be turned in. They should never be started or driven with a hammer because this practice tears the wood fibers and injures the screw threads, seriously reducing the load carrying capacity of the screw. Post-1991: screw lateral strength is determined by the yield model theory (Table 8-5). Modes I, III, and IV failures may occur (Fig. 8-5). The dowel bearing strength values are based on the same specific gravity equation used to establish values for nails (Eq. (8-3)). Table 8-5 prints the screw mode IV equation with 1.75 where the nail equation has 2; the handbook gives no reason for the difference.
key_points: Wood screw withdrawal: p = 108.25 G^2 D L (metric), Eq. 8-10a; for lead holes about 70% (softwoods) or 90% (hardwoods) of the root diameter and the screw sizes of Table 8-8; outside these, actual values are likely to be less (p. 8-10, 8-11)
Pre-1991 lateral: p = K D^2, Eq. 8-13, for penetration not less than seven times the shank diameter and side and main members of about the same density (p. 8-11)
Screws should always be turned in, never started or driven with a hammer (p. 8-12)
Post-1991: yield model (Table 8-5, modes I, III, IV) with dowel bearing strength from the nail equation, Eq. 8-3 (p. 8-12)
sections.applicability: Sizing and checking screwed connections for withdrawal and lateral (shear) loading.

sections.title: Lag Screws
sections.summary: Lag screw withdrawal p = 125.4 G^(3/2) D^(3/4) L (Eq. 8-14a/b) and lead holes; pre-1991 lateral resistance p = K D^2 (Eq. 8-15) with Tables 8-10 to 8-12 and the Hankinson formula (Eq. 8-16); post-1991 yield model with the bolt dowel bearing equations.
sections.body: [p. 8-12] The equations for withdrawal and lateral loads are based on lag screws having a base metal average tensile yield strength of about 310.3 MPa (45,000 lb in^-2) and an average ultimate tensile strength of 530.9 MPa (77,000 lb in^-2). The maximum direct withdrawal load of lag screws from the side grain of seasoned wood may be computed as p = 125.4 G^(3/2) D^(3/4) L (metric) (Eq. 8-14a); p = 8,100 G^(3/2) D^(3/4) L (inch-pound) (Eq. 8-14b), where p is maximum withdrawal load (N, lb), D shank diameter (mm, in.), G specific gravity based on ovendry weight and volume at 12% moisture content, and L length (mm, in.) of penetration of the threaded part. Equation (8-14) was developed independently of Equation (8-10) but gives approximately the same results. Lag screws, like wood screws, require prebored holes of the proper size (Fig. 8-8). The lead hole for the shank should be the same diameter as the shank. The diameter of the lead hole for the threaded part varies with the density of the wood: for low-density softwoods, such as the cedars and white pines, 40% to 70% of the shank diameter; for Douglas-fir and Southern Pine, 60% to 75%; and for dense hardwoods, such as oaks, 65% to 85%. In determining the withdrawal resistance, the allowable tensile strength of the lag screw at the net (root) section should not be exceeded. Penetration of the threaded part to a distance about seven times the shank diameter in the denser species (specific gravity greater than 0.61) and 10 to 12 times the shank diameter in the less dense species (specific gravity less than 0.42) will develop approximately the ultimate tensile strength of the lag screw. [p. 8-13] The resistance to withdrawal of a lag screw from the end-grain surface is about three-fourths as great as its resistance to withdrawal from the side-grain surface. Lateral resistance, pre-1991: the lateral loads for lag screws inserted in the side grain and loaded parallel to the grain of seasoned wood can be computed as p = K D^2 (Eq. 8-15), p the proportional limit lateral load parallel to grain, K from Table 8-4. The loads given by this equation apply when the thickness of the side member is 3.5 times the shank diameter, and the depth of penetration in the main member is seven times the diameter in the harder woods and 11 times the diameter in the softer woods. For other thicknesses, the computed loads should be multiplied by the factors listed in Table 8-10. The thickness of a solid wood side member should be about one-half the depth of penetration in the main member. For load perpendicular to the grain, the load should be multiplied by the factors of Table 8-11. For other angles of loading, the loads may be computed from the parallel and perpendicular values by the Hankinson formula N = P Q/(P sin^2(theta) + Q cos^2(theta)) (Eq. 8-16), where P is load or stress parallel to the grain, Q load or stress perpendicular to the grain, and N load or stress at an inclination theta with the direction of the grain. When the unthreaded shank penetrates the main member, the permitted increases in loads are given in Table 8-12. When lag screws are used with metal plates, the lateral loads parallel to the grain may be increased 25%, provided the plate thickness is sufficient so that the bearing capacity of the steel is not exceeded; no increase should be made when the applied load is perpendicular to the grain. [p. 8-14] Lag screws should not be used in end grain, because splitting may develop under lateral load; if so used, the loads should be taken as two-thirds those for lateral resistance when lag screws are inserted into side grain and the loads act perpendicular to the grain. Spacings, end and edge distances, and net section should be the same as for joints with bolts of a diameter equal to the shank diameter. Lag screws should always be inserted by turning with a wrench, not by driving with a hammer. Post-1991: lag screw lateral strength is determined by the yield model theory table similar to the procedure for bolts. Modes I, III, and IV yield may occur (Fig. 8-5). The dowel bearing strength values are based on the same parallel- and perpendicular-to-grain specific gravity equations used to establish values for bolts (Eq. 8-17, 8-18). For other angles of loading, the dowel bearing strength is determined by the Hankinson equation.
key_points: Lag screw withdrawal: p = 125.4 G^(3/2) D^(3/4) L (metric), Eq. 8-14a; 8,100 G^(3/2) D^(3/4) L (inch-pound), Eq. 8-14b; the net (root) section tensile strength should not be exceeded (p. 8-12)

Pre-1991 lateral parallel to grain: p = K D^2, Eq. 8-15, for side member 3.5 D and penetration 7 D (harder) or 11 D (softer); Table 8-10 for other thicknesses, Table 8-11 for perpendicular to grain (p. 8-13)
Hankinson formula, Eq. 8-16: N = P Q/(P sin^2(theta) + Q cos^2(theta)) (p. 8-13)
Lag screws should not be used in end grain; they should always be inserted by turning with a wrench, not by driving with a hammer (p. 8-14)
Post-1991: dowel bearing strength from the bolt equations (parallel and perpendicular to grain), not the nail equation (p. 8-14)
sections.applicability: Heavy connections (ledger attachment, hardware-to-timber connections) using lag screws.

sections.title: Bolts
sections.summary: Bolts: bearing stress under bolts (Figs. 8-9 to 8-13), loads at an angle to grain (Hankinson equation), steel side plates, bolt quality, member thickness, multiple-member joints, spacing and edge and end distance, bolt holes, the pre-1991 allowable loads and the post-1991 European Yield Model with bolt dowel bearing strengths Fe = 77.2 G parallel (Eq. 8-17a/b) and 212.0 G^1.45 D^-0.5 perpendicular to grain (Eq. 8-18a/b).
sections.body: [p. 8-14] The bearing stress under a bolt is computed by dividing the load on a bolt by the product LD, where L is the length of a bolt in the main member and D is the bolt diameter. Prior to 1991, bearing stress was based on test results at the proportional limit; since 1991, bearing stress is based on test results at a yield limit state, which is defined as the 5% diameter offset on the load-deformation curve (similar to Fig. 8-4). The curves of Figures 8-9 and 8-10 show the reduction in proportional limit bolt-bearing stress as L/D increases. The proportional limit bolt-bearing stress parallel to grain for small L/D ratios is approximately 50% of the small clear crushing strength for softwoods and approximately 60% for hardwoods. [p. 8-15] Loads at an angle to the grain: for other angles of loading, the dowel bearing strength values for use in the yield model are determined by the Hankinson equation, where P and Q are the values of dowel bearing parallel and perpendicular to grain, respectively. Steel side plates: when steel side plates are used, the bolt-bearing stress parallel to grain at joint proportional limit is approximately 25% greater than that for wood side plates. Bolt quality: the percentages given in Figures 8-9 and 8-10 for calculating bearing stress apply to steel machine bolts with a yield stress of 310 MPa (45,000 lb in^-2); Figure 8-12 indicates the increase in bearing stress parallel to grain for bolts with a yield stress of 862 MPa (125,000 lb in^-2). Member thickness: pre-1991 design values for bolts are based on joints with the side member half the thickness of the main member (Fig. 8-13); [p. 8-16] post-1991 design values include member thickness directly in the yield model equations. Post-1991 design for joints with four or more members results in values per shear plane; connection strength for any number of members is conservatively found by multiplying the value for the weakest shear plane by the number of shear planes. Spacing: the center-to-center distance along the grain should be at least four times the bolt diameter for parallel-to-grain loading. When a joint is in tension, the bolt nearest the end of a timber should be at a distance from the end of at least seven times the bolt diameter for softwoods and five times for hardwoods; when the joint is in compression, the end margin may be four times the bolt diameter for both. For bolts bearing parallel to the grain, the distance from the edge of a timber to the center of a bolt should be at least 1.5 times the bolt diameter. For parallel-to-grain loading in softwoods, the net area remaining at the critical section should be at least 80% of the total area in bearing under all the bolts in the joint; in hardwoods it should be 100%. For bolts bearing perpendicular to the grain, the margin between the edge toward which the bolt pressure is acting and the center of the bolt or bolts nearest this edge should be at least four times the bolt diameter. The prescriptive spacing requirement may not agree with a strength-based method, and the large spacing requirement should be used. Bolt holes: a bolt hole that is too large causes nonuniform bearing of the bolt; if the bolt hole is too small, the wood will split when the bolt is driven. Normally, bolts should fit so that they can be inserted by tapping lightly with a wood mallet; the smoother the hole, the higher the bearing values (Figs. 8-14, 8-15). [p. 8-17] If drying takes place after assembly of the joint, the proportional limit load for snug-fitting bolts will be considerably less due to the effects of shrinkage. Pre-1991 allowable loads were derived from the 5% exclusion value of green crushing strength (parallel) or the average green proportional limit stress in compression perpendicular to grain (perpendicular), with the factors and Tables 8-13 to 8-15. Post-1991 yield model: the empirical design approach used prior to 1991 was based on a tabular value for a single bolt in a wood-to-wood, three-member connection where the side members are each a minimum of one-half the thickness of the main member; the single-bolt value must then be modified for any variation from these reference conditions. The theoretical approach, after 1991, is more general and is not limited to these reference conditions. It is based on work done in Europe (Johansen 1949) and is referred to as the European Yield Model (EYM). [p. 8-19] Dowel bearing strength for bolts: parallel to grain Fe = 77.2 G (metric) (Eq. 8-17a), Fe = 11,200 G (inch-pound) (Eq. 8-17b); perpendicular to grain Fe = 212.0 G^1.45 D^-0.5 (metric) (Eq. 8-18a), Fe = 6,100 G^1.45 D^-0.5 (inch-pound) (Eq. 8-18b), where Fe is dowel bearing strength (MPa, lb in^-2), G specific gravity based on ovendry weight and volume, and D bolt diameter (mm, in.) (the exponents are printed as "1 45" and "-0 5", the decimal points not shown).
key_points: Bolt dowel bearing strength parallel to grain: Fe = 77.2 G (metric), Eq. 8-17a; 11,200 G (inch-pound), Eq. 8-17b (p. 8-19)
Bolt dowel bearing strength perpendicular to grain: Fe = 212.0 G^1.45 D^-0.5 (metric), Eq. 8-18a; 6,100 G^1.45 D^-0.5 (inch-pound), Eq. 8-18b (p. 8-19)
Other angles of loading: dowel bearing strength by the Hankinson equation (p. 8-15)

End distance in tension at least 7 D (softwoods) or 5 D (hardwoods), 4 D in compression; along-grain spacing at least 4 D; edge distance at least 1.5 D parallel, 4 D toward the loaded edge perpendicular to grain (p. 8-16)
Steel side plates: bolt-bearing stress parallel to grain at proportional limit approximately 25% greater than with wood side plates (p. 8-15)
sections.applicability: Bolted timber connection design, and any wood bearing/loading problem at an angle to the grain. No function codes the bolt dowel bearing strengths, Eqs. 8-17 and 8-18; fastenings.yield_limit_lateral_strength takes nails and screws only and uses the nail equation, Eq. 8-3, so it does not cover bolts.

sections.title: Connector Joints (Split Rings and Shear Plates)
sections.summary: Split-ring and shear-plate connector joints: load parallel and perpendicular to grain varies linearly with specific gravity (Figs. 8-18 to 8-23); design loads from ultimate loads divided by about 4 (parallel) or from proportional limit loads (perpendicular); species groups (Table 8-17), design loads (Table 8-18) and modifications.
sections.body: [p. 8-19] Connectors increase joint bearing and shear areas by utilizing rings or plates around bolts holding joint members together. The primary load-carrying portions of these joints are the connectors; the bolts usually serve to prevent transverse separation of the members but do contribute some load-carrying capacity. Loads for wood joints with steel connectors, split ring (Fig. 8-16) and shear plate (Fig. 8-17), are discussed; these connectors require closely fitting machined grooves in the wood members. Parallel to grain: density of the wood is a controlling factor; for split rings, both maximum load and proportional limit load parallel to grain vary linearly with specific gravity (Figs. 8-18, 8-19); for shear plates, they vary linearly with specific gravity for the less dense species (Figs. 8-20, 8-21), and in the higher density species the shear strength of the bolts becomes the controlling factor. [p. 8-20] Perpendicular to grain: for split rings, the proportional limit loads perpendicular to grain are 58% of the parallel-to-grain proportional limit loads, with joint deformation at proportional limit 30% to 50% more; for shear plates, the proportional limit and maximum loads vary linearly with specific gravity (Figs. 8-22, 8-23). Design loads for parallel-to-grain loading have been established by dividing ultimate test loads by an average factor of 4, which gives values that do not exceed five-eighths of the proportional limit loads; design loads for normal duration of load are 10% higher. For perpendicular-to-grain loading, for split rings the proportional limit load is reduced by approximately half; for shear plates the design loads are approximately five-eighths of the proportional limit test loads. Species groupings are in Table 8-17 and design loads (for long-continued load) in Table 8-18. Steel side plates with shear plates give loads parallel to grain approximately 10% higher than wood side plates; perpendicular-to-grain loads are unchanged. [p. 8-21] If the wood will be more or less continuously damp or wet in use, two-thirds of the tabulated values should be used. Where green or inadequately seasoned lumber is used with connectors, adequate maintenance measures must be adopted, including inspection and tightening of all bolts as needed while the units come to moisture equilibrium, normally during the first year. [p. 8-23] Further modifications cover net section, end distance and spacing, placement of multiple connectors, cross bolts and multiple-fastener joints (Figs. 8-24, 8-25).
key_points: Split-ring loads parallel to grain vary linearly with specific gravity; for shear plates in denser species the bolt shear strength controls (p. 8-19)
Split-ring proportional limit load perpendicular to grain is 58% of the parallel value (p. 8-20)
Design loads parallel to grain: ultimate test loads divided by an average factor of 4; normal duration of load design loads are 10% higher (p. 8-20)
If continuously damp or wet in use, two-thirds of the Table 8-18 values should be used (p. 8-21)
sections.applicability: Split-ring and shear-plate connector joints; the handbook gives their capacity as test curves (Figs. 8-18 to 8-23) and Table 8-18.

sections.title: Metal Plate Connectors and Joist Hangers
sections.summary: Metal plate connectors (truss plates): the design load is the smaller of the average load at 0.38 mm plate-to-wood or 0.76 mm member-to-member slip divided by 1.6 and the average ultimate load divided by 3.0. Joist hangers: design loads from ASTM D7147 tests, the smaller of the average load at 3.2 mm deformation and the average ultimate load divided by 3.0.
sections.body: [p. 8-25] Metal plate connectors, commonly called truss plates, transmit loads by means of teeth, plugs, or nails, which vary from manufacturer to manufacturer (Fig. 8-26). Basic strength values for plate connectors are determined from load-slip curves from tension tests of two butted wood members joined with two plates (Fig. 8-27). Design values are expressed as load per tooth, nail, plug, or unit area of plate. The smallest value as determined by two different means is the design load for normal duration of load: (1) the average load of at least five specimens at 0.38-mm (0.015-in.) slip from plate to wood member or 0.76-mm (0.030-in.) slip from member to member is divided by 1.6; (2) the average ultimate load of at least five specimens is divided by 3.0. The strength of a metal plate joint may also be controlled by the tensile or shear strength of the plate. Joist hangers are usually made of light-gauge steel or welded from plate steel; loads are transmitted from the joist to the hanger primarily through direct bearing of the joist, but for the uplift forces, load transfer is due to lateral loading of fasteners. [p. 8-26] Face-mount hangers transmit loads through lateral loading of dowel-type fasteners; top-mount hangers by bearing on the top of the header and lateral loading of the dowel type fasteners. Design loads are limited to the lowest values determined by experiment or by calculations. By experiment, design loads for joist hangers are determined from tests in which a joist is loaded at midspan and supported by two joist hangers attached to headers, following ASTM D7147 procedures. The smallest value as determined by two different means is the test design load for normal duration of load: (1) the average load at 3.2-mm (0.125-in.) deformation between the joist and header of at least six specimens and (2) the average ultimate load of at least six specimens divided by 3.0 or the least ultimate load for lower than six replicates divided by 3.0. Design loads for calculations are also highlighted in ASTM D7147.
key_points: Metal plate connector design load (normal duration): the smaller of (1) the average load of at least five specimens at 0.38 mm plate-to-wood or 0.76 mm member-to-member slip divided by 1.6 and (2) the average ultimate load of at least five specimens divided by 3.0 (p. 8-25)

Joist hanger test design load (ASTM D7147): the smaller of (1) the average load at 3.2 mm joist-to-header deformation of at least six specimens and (2) the average ultimate load of at least six specimens divided by 3.0 (p. 8-26)
sections.applicability: Truss plate and joist hanger design loads from tests.

sections.title: Fastener Head Embedment
sections.summary: Embedment of a fastener head (e.g., nail or screw head pulling through sheathing) is characterized empirically by maximum embedment load vs. fastener perimeter (Fig 8-29) and load at a specified embedment vs. bearing area (Fig 8-30), by species.
sections.body: [p. 8-26] The bearing strength of wood under fastener heads is important in such applications as the anchorage of building framework to foundation structures. The fastening loads could cause tensile failure of the fastenings, withdrawal of the fastenings from the framing member, or embedment of the fastener heads in the member; the fastener head could even be pulled completely through. The maximum load for fastener head embedment is related to the fastener head perimeter, whereas loads at low embedments (1.27 mm (0.05 in.)) are related to the fastener head bearing area. These relations for several species at 10% moisture content are shown in Figures 8-29 and 8-30. When annularly threaded nails are used for withdrawal applications, fastener head embedment or pull-through can be a limiting condition and should be considered in design.
key_points: Maximum head embedment load relates to the fastener head perimeter; load at 1.27 mm embedment relates to the head bearing area (Figs. 8-29, 8-30, 10% moisture content) (p. 8-26)
With annularly threaded nails in withdrawal, head embedment or pull-through can be a limiting condition and should be considered in design (p. 8-26)
sections.applicability: Fastener head pull-through, e.g. anchorage of framing to foundations and threaded nails in withdrawal.
